row.name: Dolphin Chimney
gear: Rack to a #5 cam (roughly 3.5 to 6 inches) — the size published descriptions call for on this pitch
A #6 can back up the first 20 feet below the chockstone, but parties who've climbed it don't trust it as solid pro there
Only a few thin nuts and small cams protect around the chockstone itself — expect real gaps, not just tight spacing
Gear improves markedly above the roof, on the wild exit moves — good placements return once you're through
Rated 5.9+ R, so chimney/offwidth technique carries more of the safety margin than the rack size does
hazards: Rated R — minimal protection for most of the pitch
row.overview: A short but serious offwidth/chimney pitch on SEWS — the unmistakable dark chasm midway up the wall, directly left of the Boving Roofs. Often climbed as a variation linking into the Southwest Rib rather than as a full independent route to the summit. First ascended by Fred Beckey and Jim Madsen in 1967.
row.beta: An amazing and unique offwidth/chimneying experience on great rock, transitioning from chimneying to slab moves near the top; the chimney narrows from about 2 ft to 1 ft near the exit. Backpacks can be hauled from the belay.
row.turnaround: A short, serious single-pitch route - the main hazard is the runout (R) rating rather than time, so assess conditions and confidence before committing.
row.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
row.comms: No cell service at Washington Pass.
row.descent: Rejoins the Southwest Rib's final slabby arete pitch to the summit; descend via the South Arete.

row.detailed_rack: Wide gear for the offwidth/chimney section (large cams) plus a standard rack for the exit sequence, where good placements appear near the roof.
what_to_bring: confidence on runout, unprotected chimney terrain
pro_tips: Packs can be hauled from the belay rather than climbed with, given the chimney's tight dimensions.
row.watch_out:
Sustained 5.9+ climbing in chimney terrain with exposure
Chimney sections can trap loose rock which falls on climbers below
Route-finding near chimney exit critical; easy to commit to wrong line
Weather hazard - afternoon storms on exposed sections
Descent requires careful rope management through chimney sections
row.pro_needs: Sparse, committing protection — a serious lead given the R rating and lack of good gear in the lower chimney.
row.best_season: Late June through September, dry rock.
row.approach: Start from the Blue Lake Trailhead on Highway 20 just west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail roughly 1.25 miles (about an hour of easy hiking, modest gain) to the open meadow/clearing on the northwest side of the Liberty Bell massif marked by a wooden trail sign. Leave the maintained trail here and follow the well-worn climber's path up through talus and heather benches into the basin below South Early Winters Spire's west side. Continue up the scree/boulder slope toward the base of the Southwest Rib / Boving-Pollock start (the Y-shaped larch tree left of the southwest couloir is the landmark most parties use). Dolphin Chimney itself is not started from the ground — it is gained by climbing the first 2-3 pitches of the Southwest Rib or Northwest Face (Boving-Pollock), then traversing left over easy terrain to the obvious dark, unmistakable chasm about 100 ft left of the Boving Roof.
row.descent_text: Dolphin Chimney is a single spectacular ~75 ft pitch (5.9+ R), not a full line to the summit, so it is normally done as a one-pitch add-on within a Southwest Rib / Boving-Pollock day rather than climbed and descended on its own. Most parties either continue past it on easier cracks to rejoin the Southwest Rib and finish to the summit, then take the standard South Early Winters Spire descent: downclimb the South Arete (3rd/4th class with one short, more exposed step) to the 'Rabbit Ears' — two boulder towers with fixed rappel slings — then make a short traverse/downclimb into the descent gully and do 3 single-rope rappels (60m rope) from bolted anchors/chains to the base, finishing on scree back to the climber's trail and Blue Lake Trail. If a party climbs the Dolphin as an out-and-back pitch, expect to lower or make a single rappel back to the ledge below rather than continue up. Given the offwidth/chimney nature of the pitch and sparse gear noted by climbers, rope management on any rappel of the chimney itself deserves extra care.
row.bail: Limited protection makes retreat from mid-pitch difficult; commit only with confidence on wide/chimney terrain.

pitch_detail.notes: Offwidth/chimney narrowing to 1-2 ft near the top; limited gear until the roof exit.

Start from the Blue Lake Trailhead on Highway 20 just west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail roughly 1.25 miles, about an hour of easy hiking at modest gain, to the open meadow and clearing on the northwest side of the Liberty Bell massif, marked by a WOODEN TRAIL SIGN. approach_variants.baseFinding:
DOLPHIN CHIMNEY IS NOT STARTED FROM THE GROUND. It is gained by climbing the FIRST TWO OR THREE PITCHES of the Southwest Rib or the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, then TRAVERSING LEFT OVER EASY TERRAIN TO THE OBVIOUS DARK, UNMISTAKABLE CHASM ABOUT 100 FT LEFT OF THE BOVING ROOF.

SO THE FEATURE ITSELF IS THE TEST AND IT IS AS GOOD AS THEY GET ON THIS WALL: A DARK CHASM. Not a crack, not a corner, and not something you could talk yourself into. If you are unsure whether you are looking at it, you are not looking at it.

THE MEASURED OFFSET GIVES A SECOND CHECK: ABOUT 100 FT LEFT OF THE BOVING ROOF. The Boving Roofs pitch is the double-roof feature reached by going left at a ledge from the same rib. Two roofs stacked above you, then a hundred feet further left, is the chimney.

THE GROUND-LEVEL AIMING POINT FOR THE WHOLE DAY: THE Y-SHAPED LARCH TREE LEFT OF THE SOUTHWEST COULOIR, at the base of the Southwest Rib. That is the landmark most parties use to start up this wall, and it is the one thing here you can find at ground level.

HOW THIS ROUTE IS ACTUALLY DONE, WHICH SHOULD SHAPE THE PLAN: it is a one-pitch add-on within a Southwest Rib or Boving-Pollock day, not a climb with its own descent. Most parties continue past it on easier cracks to rejoin the Southwest Rib and finish to the summit, then take the standard South Arete descent to the RABBIT EARS, two boulder towers with fixed rappel slings, then a short traverse and downclimb into the descent gully and three single-rope 60 m rappels to the base. A party doing the Dolphin as an out-and-back lowers or makes a single rappel back to the ledge below.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
bivy.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground
bivy.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
bivy.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
bivy.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
bivy.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

The rack, protection and approach text are reworded to put the glacier gear on the ice cap and flanks rather than the approach.

earlier_research.fact: Distance to the base of the ridge
earlier_research.correct_value: The ridge is gained almost immediately above camp; the 7-mile figure is unsupported

Dispute is only with the shared High Camp bivy card. Sources show a meadow stream at High Camp that may stop running late in summer, and a glacial lake above camp where parties fill up, so 'last reliable water' at East Fork Adams Creek is defensible while the card's 'reliable through summer' is overstated; left to the camping clean-up.

A guide service says the steepest sections of the North Ridge are around 40 degrees, and a route listing gives a maximum slope of about 40 degrees. The itinerary's 'around 40°' is right and max_angle 50 is the outlier.

No outside source found giving a recommended departure time for this route (one traverse party started at 7 a.m. from the car, which does not bear on a camp start). A published route description stating a start window would settle 2-3 AM vs 3-4 AM.

siblings.name: North Face of the Northwest Ridge

row.name: North Ridge
row.fa: A.G. Aiken, Edward J. Allen, and Andrew J. Burge, 1854 (first ascent of Mount Adams)
hazards: Steep, sustained snow on the upper ridge with rockfall from the ridge crest
Crevasses on the Adams and Lava glaciers either side of the ridge
Remote north-side approach — long self-reliant day
row.overview: Also called the North Cleaver, the North Ridge is Adams' second most-popular summit route and a scenic, less-crowded alternative to the South Climb. It climbs the rock-and-snow rib between the Adams and Lava Glaciers, reached via the quiet Killen Creek approach on the north side, and is most pleasant early season while still largely snow-covered.
row.beta: From high camp near the Adams Glacier moraine, gain the North Ridge (North Cleaver) and follow it upward, bypassing most obstacles on either side, to the summit ice cap; traverse roughly a mile across the plateau to reach the true summit.
row.turnaround: Turn around by midday on the upper ridge if snow is softening or weather builds; the descent is long.
row.permit: Mt. Adams Climbing Pass (Cascade Volcano Pass) required above 7,000 ft May 1-Sep 30, sold per trip on Recreation.gov; free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead otherwise. Pack out human waste.
row.comms: Cell coverage is limited to absent on this side of the mountain.
row.descent: Retrace route via North Ridge and Lava Glacier back to high camp.

sectionBreakdown.note: Hike the Killen Creek Trail through forest, meadow, and huckleberry fields, crossing East Fork Adams Creek (last reliable water) before climbing onto snow to High Camp at about 6,900 ft.
Alpine start up steep sections to around 40°, gaining the ridge and the summit plateau, then reversing the route back to High Camp. Parties who stage a shuttle car at Cold Springs …
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Summit via the North Ridge, return to camp

sectionBreakdown.note: Break camp and hike back down the Killen Creek Trail to the trailhead.

row.detailed_rack: Per person: ice axe (second tool useful in firm conditions), crampons, helmet, harness. Per team: 30–40 m rope, 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit for the summit ice cap.
pro_tips: Use the Killen Creek approach and camp at High Camp for the best base
Plan a South Spur descent and arrange transport between trailheads
Go early season for firm snow and filled-in crevasses
Start early to climb the steep snow before it softens
watch_out: Moderate snow climbing at high elevation
Water availability at notch dependent on seasonal snowmelt
row.pro_needs: Snow protection (pickets) for the steeper upper ridge plus glacier-travel gear for the summit ice cap; generally no rock pro.
row.best_season: June to mid-July for firm snow and minimized rockfall/crevasse hazard.
row.approach: Killen Creek Trailhead (Trail #113, off FR 2329 via FR 23) climbs through forest and meadow ~3.1 mi/1,400 ft to the PCT, then continues to High Camp — roughly 4 mi and 2,300 ft of gain total from the trailhead — the shared base camp for the North Ridge, Adams Glacier, and Northwest Ridge routes.
row.descent_text: Most parties descend the route itself, back down the North Ridge toward high camp; it is non-technical, mostly Class 2 over loose volcanic scree. Some parties instead carry over and descend the South Climb to Cold Springs, which requires a long car shuttle. Watch crevasses on any glacier descent.
row.bail: High Camp on the north side is the bail/base point; retreat down the ridge or glacier toward it. In poor weather the broad north-side snowfields offer non-committing descent terrain.

pitch_detail.notes: Killen Creek Trail #113 climbs through forest and meadow to the Pacific Crest Trail, then a climbers' path continues to High Camp at about 6,900 ft. The last stretch crosses an exposed talus slope above a permanent snowfield. Some parties bivy higher, on scree or snow near 8,000 ft, to shorten summit day.

Head southeast from High Camp onto the foot of the North Ridge, which is gained almost right away above the camp. Early in the season snow can hide the path, so carry a compass. The approach does not require a glacier crossing.

About 2,500 ft of scrambling up rock, scree and gritty pumice, mostly Class 2 with some Class 3. Stay on the crest where you can and wind from side to side around obstacles, occasionally dropping to the west side. Rockfall is the real crux: move gently and wear a helmet. Earlier in the season there is less scree.

From around 10,000 ft the ridge turns to snowfields. One steep section has no runout and falls toward the Lava Glacier far below; crampons and an axe are needed, and it is safest while the snow is firm in the morning. On the way down it needs careful downclimbing, and a narrow rocky shelf may deserve a belay.

The ridge reaches the ice cap around 12,000 ft and the angle eases. Walk about a mile across the summit plateau to the true summit (12,276 ft). The ice cap has held small crevasses in the past, and the high point is hard to pick out in cloud, so mark the ridge exit for the descent.

days.note: Hike the Killen Creek Trail through forest, meadow, and huckleberry fields, crossing East Fork Adams Creek (last reliable water) before climbing to High Camp at about 6,900 ft.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day trip for parties without a car shuttle: ~5 hr approach to high camp, an alpine-start summit day on the North Ridge back to camp, then a hike out; with a shuttle car staged at Cold Springs, the summit-day descent can instead go straight down the South Spur, finishing in 2 days.

access.fees: $20 per person (single-trip, not annual); free for climbers under 16.
access.notes: Purchase online in advance — no cell coverage at the trailhead, so print or save the pass. Party leader enters each climber’s name and a vehicle license plate.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12. Human waste must be packed out above 7,000 ft (blue/WAG bags) — free bags available at the Trout Lake Ranger District office, no collection service. The Mazama Glacier route and Bird Creek Meadows/Round-the-Mountain area cross Yakama Nation land and require a separate small tribal recreation permit purchased at Bird Creek Meadows — the standard South Climb/Cold Springs route stays on Forest Service land and does not.
access.seasonal: South Climb route typically opens as snow melts out around May.
access.parking_pass: No trailhead parking pass is required at the Killen Creek Trailhead. The Mount Adams Climbing Pass applies separately above 7,000 ft.

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek trailhead and High Camp
approach_variants.notes:
The same walk in as the Adams Glacier and the Northwest Ridge, and High Camp is the shared base for all three. Killen Creek Trail #113 from the trailhead (~4,600 ft) runs about 3.1 miles to the PCT junction at roughly 6,100 ft; cross straight over onto High Camp Trail #10 for another mile to its end at about 6,900 ft on the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine. Camping is spread between 7,000 and 7,600 ft, including a glacial lake camp near 7,650 ft.

Access is by FR 23, 21 and 2329; FR 2329 is gravel and holds snow into early summer. East Fork Adams Creek, crossed about 2.5 miles up the trail, is the last dependable water.

Permits: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead, plus a Cascade Volcano Pass for travel above 7,000 ft in the summer season.

This is a longer and more committing day than the South Climb from a much quieter side of the mountain, and crevassed glacier lies on both flanks of the ridge and on the summit ice cap, so glacier skills are expected, unlike the South Spur.
approach_variants.season: June through September; a snow route early, a loose rock route once it melts out
hazards: Very loose volcanic rock the length of the ridge — helmets, and spacing between climbers
Crevassed glacier on both flanks if you leave the crest
Exposed snow travel between rock sections
Thin moraine tread above treeline, easy to lose in dark or whiteout
No running water above East Fork Adams Creek
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From High Camp the line is southeast, toward the foot of the ridge, and in clear weather you can see the whole thing from the approach — parties describe it as impossible to miss.

The recognition problem is entirely a poor-visibility one, and the test is what is under your boots. The North Ridge is the rubble-and-cinder rib that separates the Adams Glacier on its west from the Lava Glacier ground on its east. You should be on loose volcanic rock and scree, on a defined crest, with glacier falling away on BOTH sides. If you are on ice with crevasses, you have slid off the rib onto one glacier or the other, and which one tells you which way to correct.

A smooth, clean, snow-only ascent is the wrong sign on this route: it is a choss pile, and the loose rock is the confirmation rather than the complaint. Expect short easy scrambling steps low down.

The angle eases noticeably around 11,000 ft, which is the sign the ridge proper is behind you and the summit plateau ground is ahead.

bivy.name: High Camp (Adams Creek Meadows)
bivy.notes: The base for the north side, reached by the Killen Creek trail from about 4,600 ft to the PCT and then a boot path up to the meadows below the Adams Glacier. Roughly four miles and 2,300 ft of gain, an easy carry compared with the Lunch Counter, and it puts you directly under the glacier's icefall. There is no shelter from wind other than what the rock benches give you, and afternoon weather rolls in fast off the north face. Snow lingers here into July in a heavy year, which affects both the boot track and where you can pitch.
bivy.water: Generally reliable through summer. Meltwater streams from the Adams Glacier snout and small tarns feed the meadows, and Killen Creek runs lower on the approach; filter everything, and expect surface streams to shrink late in a dry season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the Killen Creek trailhead. Note the elevation carefully — at about 6,900 ft this camp sits just under the 7,000 ft threshold, so the camp itself does not require a Cascade Volcano Pass, but any climbing above that line between May 1 and Sept 30 does, so a party heading for the Adams Glacier or North Ridge needs one. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for trailhead parking. Camp on durable ground and well back from water — this is fragile subalpine meadow.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — open meadow and bench terrain with many dispersed spots; busy in wildflower season but rarely crowded by alpine standards

name: Firearms
prior_findings: Dikes (FR-64 / Middle Point): siblings were set to 'no pass needed' (fee list + tourism page); this row still carries the pass in access (check rendered fields; do not edit access._raw).

earlier_research.fact: Season window and when the FR-64 access road is open
earlier_research.correct_value: Climbing season roughly May-October (sometimes from April); FR-64 is the ski-area road and stays in use through winter — snow on the crags/approach slopes, not the road, sets the season. April-November is only the trailhead's season of use.
earlier_research.evidence: The Dikes area page gives the climbing season as May-October for most routes; the Whitman College outdoor program lists The Dikes as an April-October destination; they agree on a spring (April/May) start and an October end. April-November is the Forest Service season of use for the Middle Point trailhead itself (whose page also says forest trails are typically inaccessible late fall to late spring), not a climbing window. North Touchet Road/FR-64 continues past the Dikes to Ski Bluewood (FS directions: 19.3 mi on North Touchet Road/FR 64) and is the ski area's only surface access, so the road is in use through winter; the stored claim that the road is only snow-free mid-June to October and blocked in winter and spring is unsupported and contradicts both climbing-season sources.

The Umatilla NF passes page says the NW Forest Pass applies only at Forest Service sites where a day-use fee is charged; a search summary of the forest's day-use fee list named Elk Flats, Jubilee Lake, Meadow Creek, Panjab, Teepee, Three Forks, Timothy Springs, Tucannon and Twin Buttes (not Middle Point or any FR-64 pullout), and the Middle Point Trailhead page lists no fee. That points to the rendered 'no pass' fields being right, but it is one publisher and the fee list itself could not be fetched to confirm; web tools hit their limit. Note other Dikes rows in this batch render 'Northwest Forest Pass' as required, a cross-route disagreement for the same pullouts.

The Umatilla NF day-use fee list and the Region 6 fee-site list both name only nine Umatilla fee sites (Elk Flats, Jubilee Lake, Meadow Creek, Panjab, Teepee, Three Forks, Timothy Springs, Tucannon, Twin Buttes); neither lists Middle Point or any FR 64 pullout, and the Middle Point Trailhead page states no fee. That supports the rendered 'no pass' fields, but both lists come from one publisher (the Forest Service); the climbing area page and the crag guide (unreachable) say nothing about passes. The disputed values live only in access._raw, which does not render. Would settle: an independent climbing or local source stating no pass is needed at the Dikes pullouts.

earlier_research.fact: Driving distance from Dayton to the crag
earlier_research.correct_value: The Middle Point Ridge Trailhead is 16-17 mi from Dayton and the dikes cross the road 1.1-1.5 mi beyond it, so the crag is ~18 mi from Dayton, not 20 and not 16-17
earlier_research.evidence: The Forest Service gives 1.5 mi on S 4th St plus ~15 mi on North Touchet Road (~16.5 mi) to Middle Point Trailhead; WTA gives 16.9 mi from downtown Dayton; the Dikes climbing guide says 16-17 mi from the Hwy 12 turn and puts the megadike/minidike parking 1.1-1.5 mi past the trailhead (The Castle parking 1.2 mi back down the road). The row's own trailhead and Megadike pins are ~1.1 mi apart. So 20 mi overstates it, and the 16-17 mi in road.status/access.notes is the trailhead distance, not the crag distance (road.status even says 16-17 mi AND 1-2 mi past the trailhead).

waypoints.name: Middle Point Trailhead (FR 64)
waypoints.note: Drive ~1.5 miles further south on FR 64 past this trailhead, then a short scramble up to Minidike's base.
waypoints.directions: From Dayton, follow North Touchet Road out of town toward Ski Bluewood; it is paved for roughly the first 15 to 16 miles, then turns to gravel as Forest Service Road 64 at the national forest boundary. The Dikes sit along that road in the East Fork Touchet River valley below Ski Bluewood, in the Walla Walla Ranger District of the Umatilla National Forest. The road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter; snow on the crags and approach slopes is what limits climbing, to roughly May through October, sometimes from April. You do not park at this trailhead: for the Minidike, keep driving about 1.5 miles further south on FR 64 past it and park on the left, southeast side of the road just after you cross the bridge over the river.

waypoints.name: Minidike
waypoints.note: Smaller of the two closely-spaced fins at the core of The Dikes; park ~1.5 mi past the trailhead just after the river bridge, cross the road, scramble down the abutment, and follow the trail downstream on the NW bank.

row.detailed_rack: 7 bolts to chain anchors, shared with Cheap Beer.
pro_tips: Use the good rest point before the chains to shake out on the overhanging start
watch_out: Overhanging opening moves — pace yourself before the rest
row.best_season: Roughly May through October, sometimes from April.
row.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on the Minidike: park 1.5 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead on the left (SE) side of the road, just after crossing a bridge over the river. Cross the road, scramble down the bridge abutment, and follow a trail downstream on the NW side.
row.bail: Fully bolted; lower from any bolt.

pitch_detail.notes: Overhanging start eases to a good rest before the shared chain anchor (7 bolts).

name: Internal Combustion
prior_findings: Dikes (FR-64 / Middle Point): siblings were set to 'no pass needed'; this row still carries the pass (check rendered fields; do not edit access._raw).

earlier_research.fact: Season window and when the FR-64 access road is open
earlier_research.correct_value: Climbing season roughly May-October (sometimes from April); FR-64 is the ski-area road and stays in use through winter — snow on the crags/approach slopes, not the road, sets the season. April-November is only the trailhead's season of use.
earlier_research.evidence: The Dikes area page gives the climbing season as May-October for most routes; the Whitman College outdoor program lists The Dikes as an April-October destination; they agree on a spring (April/May) start and an October end. April-November is the Forest Service season of use for the Middle Point trailhead itself (whose page also says forest trails are typically inaccessible late fall to late spring), not a climbing window. North Touchet Road/FR-64 continues past the Dikes to Ski Bluewood (FS directions: 19.3 mi on North Touchet Road/FR 64) and is the ski area's only surface access, so the road is in use through winter; the stored claim that the road is only snow-free mid-June to October and blocked in winter and spring is unsupported and contradicts both climbing-season sources.

The Umatilla NF passes page says the NW Forest Pass applies only at Forest Service sites where a day-use fee is charged; a search summary of the forest's day-use fee list named Elk Flats, Jubilee Lake, Meadow Creek, Panjab, Teepee, Three Forks, Timothy Springs, Tucannon and Twin Buttes (not Middle Point or any FR-64 pullout), and the Middle Point Trailhead page lists no fee. That points to the rendered 'no pass' fields being right, but it is one publisher and the fee list itself could not be fetched to confirm; web tools hit their limit. Note other Dikes rows in this batch render 'Northwest Forest Pass' as required, a cross-route disagreement for the same pullouts.

The Umatilla NF day-use fee list and the Region 6 fee-site list both name only nine Umatilla fee sites (Elk Flats, Jubilee Lake, Meadow Creek, Panjab, Teepee, Three Forks, Timothy Springs, Tucannon, Twin Buttes); neither lists Middle Point or any FR 64 pullout, and the Middle Point Trailhead page states no fee. That supports the rendered 'no pass' fields, but both lists come from one publisher (the Forest Service); the climbing area page and the crag guide (unreachable) say nothing about passes. The disputed values live only in access._raw, which does not render. Would settle: an independent climbing or local source stating no pass is needed at the Dikes pullouts.

earlier_research.fact: Driving distance from Dayton to the crag
earlier_research.correct_value: The Middle Point Ridge Trailhead is 16-17 mi from Dayton and the dikes cross the road 1.1-1.5 mi beyond it, so the crag is ~18 mi from Dayton, not 20 and not 16-17
earlier_research.evidence: The Forest Service gives 1.5 mi on S 4th St plus ~15 mi on North Touchet Road (~16.5 mi) to Middle Point Trailhead; WTA gives 16.9 mi from downtown Dayton; the Dikes climbing guide says 16-17 mi from the Hwy 12 turn and puts the megadike/minidike parking 1.1-1.5 mi past the trailhead (The Castle parking 1.2 mi back down the road). The row's own trailhead and Megadike pins are ~1.1 mi apart. So 20 mi overstates it, and the 16-17 mi in road.status/access.notes is the trailhead distance, not the crag distance (road.status even says 16-17 mi AND 1-2 mi past the trailhead).

row.name: Internal Combustion
hazards: Talus approach and fractured basalt typical of the Dikes
row.overview: The last route on the Minidike face, a little up the talus; juggy start building to a technical crux near the top.
row.beta: Begins with juggy holds and progresses through increasingly technical movement. The crux comes right before the last bolt, with an option to move right or take a recently-cleaned left-side slot finish. Anchors sit 6 ft above the final bolt, partly hidden behind small trees.
row.turnaround: Short, fully bolted single pitch — the notable hazard is loose talus underfoot at the base rather than a time-based turnaround.
row.descent: Lower from the chain anchor (8 bolts) on a single strand.

waypoints.name: Middle Point Trailhead (FR 64)
waypoints.note: Drive ~1.5 miles further south on FR 64 past this trailhead, then a short scramble up to Minidike's base.
waypoints.directions: From Dayton, follow North Touchet Road out of town toward Ski Bluewood; it is paved for roughly the first 15 to 16 miles, then turns to gravel as Forest Service Road 64 at the national forest boundary. The Dikes sit along that road in the East Fork Touchet River valley below Ski Bluewood, in the Walla Walla Ranger District of the Umatilla National Forest. The road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter; snow on the crags and approach slopes is what limits climbing, to roughly May through October, sometimes from April. You do not park at this trailhead: for the Minidike, keep driving about 1.5 miles further south on FR 64 past it and park on the left, southeast side of the road just after you cross the bridge over the river.

waypoints.name: Minidike
waypoints.note: Smaller of the two closely-spaced fins at the core of The Dikes; park ~1.5 mi past the trailhead just after the river bridge, cross the road, scramble down the abutment, and follow the trail downstream on the NW bank.

row.detailed_rack: 8 bolts to chains, set 6 ft above the final bolt behind small trees.
pro_tips: Crux is right before the last bolt — a recently-cleaned left-side slot finish is an alternative to moving right
watch_out: Anchors are partly hidden behind small trees — look carefully above the last bolt
row.best_season: Roughly May through October, sometimes from April.
row.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on the Minidike: park 1.5 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead on the left (SE) side of the road, just after crossing a bridge over the river. Cross the road, scramble down the bridge abutment, and follow a trail downstream on the NW side.
row.bail: Fully bolted; lower from any bolt.

pitch_detail.notes: Juggy start builds to a technical crux just below the last bolt; finish right or via a cleaned left-side slot to chains hidden behind small trees.

_raw.special_hazards: Climbing rock (check current condition via climbing guides)
_raw.permit_cost_structure: Day use only; NW Forest Pass $5 (5-day) or $30 (annual)

access.fees: No developed-trailhead fee at these roadside pullouts -- the approaches are informal, unofficial parking spots along FR-64, not a developed fee site.
access.notes: A basalt "cordwood-jointed" dike/fin formation in the East Fork Touchet River valley off FS Rd 64, ~18 mi south of Dayton, WA. Unmaintained approach, seasonally snowed in late fall through spring.
access.permit: No permit required for day climbing at these informal roadside pullouts.
access.closures: FR-64 (Bluewood Road) stays in use through winter as the road to Ski Bluewood, but snow on the crags and approach slopes limits climbing to roughly May through October; check with the Walla Walla Ranger District before a winter/spring trip.
access.permitZone: Not in designated wilderness -- Blue Mountains, East Fork Touchet River valley

road.name: Touchet Road / FR-64 (Bluewood Road) from Dayton
road.status: Paved North Touchet Road out of Dayton becomes gravel-to-dirt Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary as it climbs toward the Bluewood ski area; the climbing dikes sit right along this road roughly 18 miles in (about 1-2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, which is 16-17 miles from Dayton). Approach paths to individual crags (Megadike, Minidike, Weeping Wall, Joe's Rock) are unofficial, brushy, and easy to lose.
road.driveNote: Roughly 25-30 minutes (about 18 miles) from Dayton, WA via S 4th Street/North Touchet Road (FR-64).
road.seasonalGate: FR-64 continues past The Dikes to Ski Bluewood and is the ski area's only road, so it stays in use through winter; snow on the crags and approach slopes, rather than the road, limits climbing to roughly May through October, sometimes from April.
